title: VPC Crossconnect + Runtime: batching, KV cache & networking workshop
summary: Deep technical workshop covering private VPC connectivity options (PrivateLink, transit, cross-connect), DNS/eProxy patterns, NAT/hairpinning, and runtime tuning (batching, KV cache warming, quantization tradeoffs). Action items: share private deployment checklist, run KV cache warmup test, schedule on-prem crossconnect sizing call.
topics: PrivateLink vs Transit/Peering vs Direct Connect
Egress NAT hairpin and proxy patterns
DNS resolution strategies for private endpoints
KV cache warming and prefix caching
Batching policies and latency SLO tradeoffs
Quantization effects on latency and throughput

transcript:
Header: 2026-06-18 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~68min | Recording: Zoom | Location: remote
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Tom Reynolds (Redwood SE), David Kim (Redwood Infra), Maya Singh (Nexa), Carlos Ruiz (Nexa), Jules Parker (Nexa), Lina Zhao (Nexa Network)

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour and change, quick intros then jump in.
[00:14] Maya: Hi, Maya here, platform eng. We're looking to run Redwood in a private VPC, want to understand networking gotchas and runtime tuning for latency sensitive inference.
[00:22] Aisha: Perfect, Tom will lead runtime and David will do the networking deep bits.
[00:30] Tom: Cool. My plan is: start with KV cache + batching, then quantization tradeoffs, then David and Lina can take networking — PrivateLink, NAT, DNS. Questions as we go.
[00:45] Carlos: Quick note: our SLO is 95th < 40ms for short prompts; more like 100-200 token payloads.
[00:52] Tom: OK good to know. That will shape batching. We'll talk about single-request vs micro-batching and continuous batching.
[01:05] David: From a network perspective, 40ms is tight depending on cross-region hops. If you use PrivateLink inside the same AZ as the inference hosts, you can avoid transit hops.
[01:18] Lina: We currently have AWS Direct Connect to our colo, private VIF, and peering into main VPC. We prefer not to expose traffic over internet.
[01:28] Tom: That's ideal. Two patterns we usually recommend: 1) PrivateLink endpoints inside customer VPC talking to Redwood private VPC over AWS PrivateLink (cross-account NLB behind the scenes). 2) Transit/Direct Connect when you need on-prem to reach the service without hairpin.
[01:44] Maya: What's the difference in MTU/fragmentation risk between PrivateLink and Direct Connect? We saw weird timeouts previously.
[01:52] David: PrivateLink is ENI-based and uses the normal VPC path; MTU typically 1500 unless jumbo supported on DX. With Direct Connect jumbo you need to be consistent end-to-end. If MTU mismatch, you'll see odd TCP stalls which look like tail latency.
[02:12] Tom: On the runtime side, KV cache improves token generation latency by skipping recomputation for repeated prefixes. Warmup matters: first few requests incur cache misses. We recommend a warmup script that uses representative prompts to populate shard-local KV.
[02:28] Carlos: How big are the KV shards? Do they cross nodes?
[02:33] Tom: KV is sharded by model block prefix space and lives on the serving node. In dedicated deployments, shards map to GPU workers; we can further replicate hot prefixes if you need guardrails on cache miss storms.
[02:46] Maya: Replicate hot prefixes — sounds expensive. How do you balance cost vs latency?
[02:51] Tom: Two levers: replicate only top-k hot prefixes (manual or auto-detected) and use prefix-based routing to send known-hot traffic to cached nodes. That lowers overall misses. We also support TTL-based soft expiration.
[03:08] Carlos: If we do prefix routing, is there a gating requirement on sticky sessions?
[03:13] Tom: Not sticky sessions necessarily; it's more about routing keys in the request metadata. It requires your app to send a fingerprint for routing — a short hash of the prompt prefix.
[03:21] Lina: Could you show how batching interacts with KV cache? If you batch many distinct prefixes, do you lose cache hit benefits?
[03:30] Tom: Good question. Batching aggregates forward computation across requests — if prefixes differ the compute can't be fully reused, but KV cache helps within each request for autoregressive decoding. Batching helps throughput but increases tail latency if you wait too long to fill a batch. We typically recommend adaptive batching: smaller max batch for latency SLOs and adaptive timer to avoid long queues.
[03:51] Jules: What's the recommended max batch size for 40ms p95?
[03:55] Tom: It's workload dependent. For small models (7-13B) a sensible starting max_batch is 8 with a 5ms scheduling window. For bigger models 30B+, batching benefits more, but per-token compute dominates. We'll provide a table after seeing p99/latency.
[04:10] David: Network side: NAT hairpin is important for egress/back to same VPC. If customer VPC routes to an egress proxy in a different subnet, you'll see asymmetric routing unless route tables and source/destination checks are configured.
[04:27] Lina: We run an outbound proxy for logging and DLP, it's in private subnets behind an autoscaling ASG. How should that integrate?
[04:35] David: Two options: 1) Put proxy in same AZ and use route table to point 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT in each AZ; 2) Conditional DNS + split-horizon so requests to Redwood private endpoint go via PrivateLink and not the proxy. The latter avoids proxying internal traffic.
[04:52] Maya: Split-horizon DNS seems cleaner but we need audit logs on egress. How do we get those?
[04:58] David: PrivateLink hits are logged at the endpoint side; we can emit flow logs for the interface endpoints and you can pair with VPC Flow Logs + CloudWatch to capture metadata. Also Redwood can forward per-request logs to your logging endpoint with redaction. We'll share specifics.
[05:14] Tom: Back to runtime: quantization reduces model size and memory bandwidth, improving throughput, but can slightly change logits. For retrieval-sensitive apps we recommend evaluating output quality on a representative eval set. 4-bit quantization often yields good latency gains for chat workloads.
[05:34] Carlos: Any quantization interaction with KV cache?
[05:39] Tom: No direct interaction —KV cache stores key/value tensors in the serving representation. Quantization changes the compute precision, but cache storage and read semantics are consistent. However, smaller precision reduces per-token compute so you might increase batch sizes.
[05:54] Lina: For PrivateLink endpoints, what's the recommended route table / security group setup? Can we restrict by CIDR and tag?
[06:02] David: Yes. Typical pattern: create interface endpoints in consumer VPC in dedicated subnets with route tables pointing to those subnets. Security groups on ENIs allow only specific source CIDRs (your app subnets). Endpoint policies can restrict API actions. Also recommend using endpoint-specific SGs and NACLs to be explicit.
[06:20] Maya: We have SRV subnet private IPs that rotate via autoscaling. Any gotcha with ephemeral IPs and PrivateLink?
[06:27] David: No, interface endpoints are stable; your autoscaling instances just connect to the endpoint ENI IPs via DNS. Use the AWS-provided endpoint DNS name; it resolves to ENI IPs in each AZ. No need to pin individual IPs.
[06:40] Tom: One caveat: DNS TTL and caching in application or in-house resolvers can cause stale records during failover. We recommend small TTLs and health checks on both sides.
[06:52] Carlos: What about egress through customer NAT to reach Redwood? Will that add measurable latency?
[06:57] David: It can. NAT adds a hop and possible queueing; the main penalty is small but visible at tight SLOs. PrivateLink avoids NAT if calls stay internal to VPC path.
[07:10] Lina: We also use transit gateway for multi-VPC connectivity. Is PrivateLink still recommended or should we route via TGW?
[07:18] David: If you already have TGW, you can peer to the Redwood VPC via TGW attachments or use PrivateLink. PrivateLink has benefit of cross-account NLB and avoids TGW route table complexity. For on-prem, Direct Connect + TGW is often best.
[07:31] Tom: From runtime resilience: we support multi-region fallback and canary rollouts. For private deployments we can place a local region primary and fallback to a secondary region with slightly higher latency. Fallback is transparent via the Redwood SDK routing policies.
[07:48] Maya: About TLS: do we terminate TLS at the PrivateLink NLB or at the Redwood service? We're behind strict compliance rules.
[07:55] David: We support TLS end-to-end. For PrivateLink we typically use TLS from client to endpoint and mTLS onward to the service if required. We can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. We'll share TLS profiles.
[08:10] Tom: Quick interjection: warmup script pattern — sample approach is to replay 1k unique representative prompts across shards, with concurrency similar to production ramp. That primes KV cache and warms CUDA kernels so first real requests don't pay cold-start.
[08:26] Carlos: How long does kernel warmup last?
[08:29] Tom: Typically a few tens of seconds per worker for large models — but the perceived latency cost is only for the first few requests. Continuous background runner that pings with small prompts every minute helps.
[08:40] Jules: We have a compliance ask: all request logs must be retained inside our VPC. Does Redwood store anything outside?
[08:48] Aisha: For private deployments Redwood can be configured to not store PII or to forward logs into your logging endpoints. We have a Private deployment mode where control plane sits in your VPC and telemetry stays on-prem. We'll send the specific SOC2/ISO snippets.
[09:00] Maya: On the routing key for prefix-based routing, can we compute it client-side deterministically?
[09:05] Tom: Yes, we provide a small SDK helper that hashes a prefix and sends an afferent header like X-Redwood-Prefix-Hash. The routing layer uses that to route to hot nodes.
[09:15] Lina: We worry about egress DNS for private endpoints. Our resolver is in VPC and does conditional forwarding to on-prem DNS. Will Redwood's endpoint DNS play nicely?
[09:24] David: As long as your resolver forwards the AWS-provided endpoint domains, you'll be fine. If you have a DNS forwarder that doesn't respect split-horizon, you may end up resolving to public IPs — avoid that. Use the AWS endpoint private DNS names with VPC endpoints enabled.
[09:38] Tom: Back to batching: adaptive batching parameters we often tune: max_batch_size, max_queue_ms, and token-level preemption. Preemption allows urgent single requests to bypass batch waiting. That helps p95.
[09:51] Carlos: Token-level preemption sounds complex to implement in our client. Is it server side?
[09:56] Tom: Server side — you only flag priority in request metadata and the scheduler handles preemption. We'll show examples in the snippet.
[10:05] Maya: Can you talk about autoscaling and how it interacts with cache locality? If workers come and go we might lose warm KV state.
[10:13] Tom: Great point. Two patterns: 1) Sticky worker pool for hot traffic (min capacity), 2) Fast scale with background warmup to rehydrate KV caches. We also support shard replication for critical prefixes so new nodes are seeded. Replication has cost but lowers tail during scale events.
[10:30] Jules: Any instrumentation you provide to measure cache hit rate and cold-starts?
[10:34] Tom: Yes — Console shows request-level cache hit rates, per-shard hit ratio, decode latencies. We also emit traces that you can pipe into your APM.
[10:44] Lina: On network ACLs, do you recommend stateful security groups or NACLs for interface endpoints?
[10:49] David: Security groups are stateful and easier. NACLs are stateless and can be used for additional layer. Keep SG rules minimal and use endpoint policies for further restriction.
[10:58] Carlos: For the crossconnect bandwidth — if we plan 10Gbps to start, do you recommend colocating Redwood nodes in same region?
[11:05] David: Yes, for predictable throughput you want region-local serving. We'll size GPU pools based on tokens/sec targets. If you start 10Gbps, we can provision dedicated capacity with predictable throughput.
[11:18] Tom: Regarding quantization again: some kernels perform best with 8-bit matrix multiplies; others with int4 depending on model architecture. Our runtime picks kernels based on model and sequence length distribution. We'll share a matrix of model->preferred quant levels.
[11:34] Maya: Are CPU-only fallbacks possible in Private deployments? For small inference bursts?
[11:38] Tom: We can provide a small CPU fallback for ultra-low-volume emergencies, but it's not latency-friendly. For production you want GPU.
[11:45] Lina: DNS caching in our resolver caused stale entries during a failover test earlier. Any Redwood guidance?
[11:51] David: Set short TTLs on endpoint records and ensure your resolver respects TTL. If you have an internal resolver with long caching, implement active health checks and flush cache on failover events.
[12:07] Tom: We should discuss test plan: recommended approach is a three-phase test: 1) Connectivity verification (DNS resolve -> TLS handshake -> small inference), 2) Load ramp with KV warmup and monitoring of p50/p95/p99, 3) Failover tests (AZ loss, node reboot) to see cache regeneration and tail.
[12:25] Maya: Sounds good. We'll need a sample harness.
[12:28] Aisha: We'll share a harness and Terraform for creating interface endpoints + sample client scripts.
[12:33] Carlos: On security - does Redwood support SAML SSO for console access and role-based access?
[12:39] Aisha: Yes, RBAC + SAML and SCIM for provisioning. For Private we can map to your IdP.
[12:44] Tom: Quick note about metrics: we recommend tracking request-level latency, batch fill time, cache hit ratio, GPU util, and network EGRESS p95.
[12:55] Lina: For egress logging, if we avoid the proxy with PrivateLink, we still want audit logs - can Redwood send request metadata into our syslog collector?
[13:04] Aisha: Yes, we can push anonymized metadata or full logs depending on contract and privacy rules. We'll include that in the checklist.
[13:14] David: A small gotcha — when you use interface endpoints across accounts, you need accept the endpoint in the provider account and ensure the NLB has the right SG. That handshake sometimes gets missed.
[13:26] Maya: We'll need the Terraform example for cross-account endpoint creation.
[13:31] Aisha: We'll include cross-account snippet and recommended IAM policy.
[13:37] Tom: Any other runtime questions?
[13:40] Carlos: One more: how do you handle model rollbacks if we see quality regressions after quantized rollout?
[13:46] Tom: Canary + auto-rollback. Redwood supports canary percentage routing and automated regression detection tied to eval prompts. If quality drops beyond threshold we trigger rollback and notify.
[13:59] Jules: That eval tie-in is critical for us. We'll need the scaffolding for our benchmark prompts.
[14:05] Tom: We'll help set that up as part of Redwood Optimize.
[14:10] Aisha: OK quick recap and next steps then wrap. We promised checklist, Terraform, KV microbenchmark, and a network sizing call.
[14:20] Maya: Thanks all.
[14:24] Aisha: Thanks, I'll follow up with materials and scheduling.
[14:30] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript has occasional transcription errors (speaker overlaps, truncated words). Some technical specifics intentionally abbreviated in the call and will be clarified in follow-up docs.
